pr_title: coredump,analyze: use read_full_file() for reading various top-level …
pr_body:
…/proc/ files

Kernel API file systems typically use either "raw" or "seq_file" to implement their various interface files. The former are really simple (to point I'd call them broken), in that they have no understanding of file offsets, and return their contents again and again on every read(), and thus EOF is indicated by a short read, not by a zero read. The latter otoh works like a typical file: you read until you get a zero-sized read back.

We have read_virtual_file() to read the "raw" files, and can use regular read_full_file() to read the "seq_file" ones.

Apparently all files in the top-level /proc/ directory use 'seq_file'. but we accidentally used read_virtual_file() for them. Fix that.

Also clarify in a comment what the rules are.

Fixes: #36131

issue_context.title: read_full_virtual_file fails to read /proc/$pid/maps correctly
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

258~devel-g1d77ac1^

### Used distribution

KDE Linux

### Linux kernel version used

6.12.9-arch1-1

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

x86_64

### Component

coredumpctl

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

COREDUMP_PROC_MAPS contains the maps at the time of the coredump

### Unexpected behaviour you saw

COREDUMP_PROC_MAPS is truncated

### Steps to reproduce the problem

SEGV an application with suitably many maps. GUI applications in general work very well, the desktop shells in particular.

Here's an example program showing the problem by comparing the output of `read_full_virtual_file` with a trivialistic reading until `read` returns 0. Needs a relevant pid put into `pid_of_large_process`.

https://gist.github.com/hsitter/9d7b69d5fae556b4e0832372ef2a78b4

```
# output of the shortread.c when run against the plasmashell pid

MAPS=4070
MAPS=388722
```

The problem in particular appears to be with `read_virtual_file_fd` assuming a short read means end of file https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/eb86b4e63bc1fd7a268a1995c2f6f8221a29ba8e/src/basic/fileio.c#L564 and that not being true for the maps file.

comments:
urks, what a mess. i don't think we can fix this generically.

see the comments about "raw" and "seq" in the function.

I think the kernel needs to fix up this area of its virtual/api filesystems.

Recently I experimented with changing the default m->size used in `fs/seq_file.c` to something smaller than PAGE_SIZE, in an effort to reduce kmem usage of some monitoring software I have which holds open ~4 /proc/$tid/... files per thread in the system.  The seq_file implementation knows how to enlarge this output buffer as needed when the producers exceed the current size, so it seemed like it should Just Work with some potential performance impact stemming from enlarging buffers.

But what I found was some of my /proc readers which were using "short read == EOF" logic similar to read_full_virtual_file were suddenly breaking, because the smaller default m->size for the seq_file was changing the size of what the userspace reads returned.  I had to put down this side-quest before digging deeper, but it suggested to me that we're already living in a broken world, dancing around the problem by virtue of most /proc files not exceeding the current PAGE_SIZE default used.  I'd always assumed as long as userspace provided a large enough buffer for the atomic read, the seq_file side would fill it as much as possible, enabling userspace to get atomic samples if it makes the effort to grow its buffer until the read is short.  That doesn't seem to always be the case when the output exceeds m->size.

If someone has time+interest in understanding this issue further on the kernel side, it'd be great if we got m->size's default size far smaller.  Most the stuff read from /proc is well under PAGE_SIZE and for performance reasons we're incentivized to hold open /proc files and always position our reads @ 0 offset for sampling.  This is pinning at least PAGE_SIZE bytes for every seq_file held open, which adds up very quickly.  I'm not sure how invasive a change on the kernel side that would actually be.  I suspect both things can happen at once if the general issue gets fixed.

I guess read_virtual_file() needs to acquire some flag we can set that controls how to interpret short reads, and then we need to carefully set that flag in the right way in the right contexts. 

Linux is sometimes so awful it hurts...
